This is one of the three headline benefits of running a hypervisor.
why_wrong: Better Utilisation is about using a server's full capacity instead of wasting it; it says nothing about what happens when a VM crashes.
Fast Disaster Recovery is the company use-case of restoring a crashed VM from a snapshot in minutes; the scenario is about the other VMs surviving, not about restoring the crashed one.
One Machine, Many OSes is the benefit that Windows and Ubuntu can share one laptop at all; the point here is that the crash did not spread, which is isolation.

questions.q: Priya installs VirtualBox on her laptop, downloads an Ubuntu Server ISO and installs it inside a new VM. In virtualisation terms, what are the laptop and the Ubuntu Server running inside the VM called, respectively?
questions.explain: The physical machine that provides the real CPU, RAM and disk is the host. Each operating system running inside a VM on top of the hypervisor is a guest. The stack is always physical host, then hypervisor, then guest OSes, so the laptop is the host and Ubuntu Server is a guest.
why_wrong: This reverses the roles: the guest is the OS living inside the VM, not the physical laptop that provides the hardware.
The hypervisor is VirtualBox itself, the software layer between host and guests; neither the laptop nor Ubuntu Server is the hypervisor.
The laptop is indeed the host, but Ubuntu Server is a guest OS running inside a VM, not the hypervisor that runs it.

questions.q: Sana has a Windows laptop and wants to try Linux for her programming course, but she cannot afford to lose Windows or any of her files. Which kind of hypervisor should she use, and why?
options: A Type 1 bare-metal hypervisor such as VMware ESXi, because it is faster
A Type 2 hosted hypervisor such as Oracle VirtualBox or VMware Workstation, because it runs on top of Windows and lets Linux run as a VM without deleting or replacing Windows
A Type 1 hypervisor such as KVM, because a Linux hypervisor is needed to run Linux guests
No hypervisor is needed; she must erase Windows and install Linux in its place
questions.explain: A hosted (Type 2) hypervisor is installed on Windows like any other application, and Linux then runs inside a virtual machine on top of it. Windows stays exactly as it is, her files are untouched, and she can delete the Linux VM at any time with no risk to the real machine. This is precisely the personal-use case that VirtualBox and VMware Workstation are built for.
why_wrong: A bare-metal hypervisor runs directly on the hardware with no host OS, so installing ESXi would mean replacing Windows rather than keeping it; speed is not the concern here.
KVM is a Type 1 bare-metal hypervisor used in data centres, and a hypervisor of either type can run Linux guests; what Sana needs is one that runs on top of her existing Windows.
That is exactly what she wants to avoid; a hosted hypervisor gives her Linux as a VM while Windows stays intact.

questions.q: A cloud provider is building a new data centre and needs each server to run as many customer VMs as possible with the highest performance. The team is deciding which hypervisor to install on the bare servers. Which choice fits, and why?
options: Oracle VirtualBox, because it is the simplest to set up
Parallels Desktop, because it supports many guest OSes side by side
A Type 1 bare-metal hypervisor such as VMware ESXi, Microsoft Hyper-V or KVM, because it runs directly on the hardware with no host OS and is faster
A Type 2 hosted hypervisor, because a host OS underneath makes each server more reliable
questions.explain: Data centres run Type 1 hypervisors: they are installed straight onto the server hardware, need no operating system underneath, and are therefore faster than hosted products. That performance is what lets one powerful server carry many VMs efficiently, which is the model AWS, Azure and Google Cloud run at massive scale. VMware ESXi, Microsoft Hyper-V, Citrix Hypervisor (XenServer) and KVM are the bare-metal options.
why_wrong: VirtualBox is a hosted Type 2 product meant for personal use; simple setup does not make up for needing a host OS underneath it on every server.
Parallels Desktop is a hosted Type 2 hypervisor for personal use; every hypervisor supports many guests, so that is not a reason to pick it for a data centre.
A host OS underneath is an extra layer that slows a hosted hypervisor down; it is the reason Type 2 is used for personal virtualisation rather than in data centres.

questions.q: Aditya uses a MacBook for college and wants to run Windows for one course tool while keeping macOS as his everyday system. Of the hypervisors covered, which product fits, and what type is it?
options: VMware ESXi, a Type 1 bare-metal hypervisor
VMware Fusion, a Type 2 hosted hypervisor
VMware Fusion, a Type 1 bare-metal hypervisor
questions.explain: VMware Fusion is the hosted hypervisor listed for the Mac: it installs as an application on macOS and runs Windows inside a VM alongside it, so macOS stays the everyday system. Because it runs on top of an existing OS it is Type 2, the type built for personal virtualisation. Its bare-metal sibling ESXi would take over the whole machine instead of living inside macOS.
why_wrong: ESXi is a bare-metal hypervisor that runs directly on the hardware with no host OS, so it would replace macOS rather than run beside it; it belongs in a data centre.
Fusion is the right product, but it is hosted on top of macOS, which makes it Type 2, not bare-metal Type 1.
KVM is a Type 1 bare-metal hypervisor used in data centres, not a hosted Mac application, and the type given here is wrong as well.

questions.q: In a lab session, Karan reads that VMware makes ESXi, Workstation and Fusion, and concludes that all three must be the same type of hypervisor. Which statement is correct?
options: All three are Type 1, because VMware is a data-centre company
All three are Type 2, because they are all installed as software
ESXi is Type 1 (bare-metal); Workstation and Fusion are Type 2 (hosted)
ESXi and Workstation are Type 1; only Fusion is Type 2 because it runs on a Mac
questions.explain: The type is decided by what the hypervisor runs on, not by who makes it. VMware ESXi installs directly on server hardware with no host OS, so it is bare-metal Type 1 and belongs in data centres. VMware Workstation and VMware Fusion (the Mac version) both run as applications on top of an existing OS, so both are hosted Type 2 products for personal use.
why_wrong: ESXi is indeed a data-centre bare-metal product, but Workstation and Fusion are hosted applications that run on top of an existing OS, which makes them Type 2.
Every hypervisor is software; the distinction is whether it runs on bare hardware (ESXi) or as an app on an existing OS (Workstation, Fusion), so they are not all Type 2.
Workstation runs on top of an existing OS just as Fusion does; running on a Mac is not what makes Fusion Type 2, being hosted on an OS is, and Workstation shares that.

questions.q: Arjun found a 'free video converter' on a random forum and wants to try it inside his Ubuntu VM. He is worried it might be malware, and he wants to be able to put the VM back exactly as it is right now in a moment if the app causes trouble. What should he do before running it?
options: Stop the VM cleanly, then start it again before installing the app
Clone the VM so a second full copy exists on disk
Take a snapshot of the VM
Delete the VM and create a fresh one after the test
questions.explain: A snapshot saves the VM's exact current state so you can return to it later. If the converter breaks something, installs malware or crashes the system, Arjun simply restores the snapshot and the VM is back to the working state it had before, with his real laptop never touched. Snapshot first, experiment second is the habit to build before trusting any unknown software.
why_wrong: Stop and Start only shut the VM down and boot it again; they save no restore point, so there would be nothing to roll back to.
Clone makes an identical second copy of the whole VM; it does not give the original VM a saved state to return to, which is exactly what a snapshot does.
Delete permanently removes the VM and frees its resources; doing it afterwards throws away his whole setup instead of returning it to the state it had before the test.

questions.q: Meera has spent a week setting up a Linux VM with every compiler, library and tool her group project needs. Her teammate Dev wants an exactly identical VM on his own laptop so they work in the same environment. Which VM management action gives Meera what she needs to hand over?
questions.explain: Clone makes an identical copy of the whole VM, its virtual disk, settings and everything installed on it, as a separate machine. That copy can be given to Dev and run on his laptop while Meera keeps her original, so both have the same environment. Cloning is how you duplicate a VM; the other actions only change the state of the one VM you already have.
why_wrong: A snapshot saves the exact state of the same VM so Meera can return to it later; it is a restore point, not a separate copy she can give to someone else.
Start only boots the VM up from where it left off; it creates nothing new.
Stop shuts the VM down cleanly; it does not produce a second copy of anything.

questions.q: A logistics company owns 10 physical servers. Each runs a single application and sits mostly idle, yet each needs its own power, cooling and space. The IT lead proposes replacing all of them with one powerful server running 10 VMs. Which reason for using hypervisors is this, and what is the payoff?
options: Safe Testing — risky updates can be tried without touching the real system
Server Consolidation — huge savings in cost and energy
Fast Disaster Recovery — a crashed VM is restored from a snapshot in minutes
Safe Isolation — if one VM crashes the others keep running
questions.explain: Server Consolidation is exactly this move: many under-used physical servers become one powerful machine running the same workloads as VMs. Because the hypervisor lets that one server use its full capacity, the company pays for and powers one box instead of ten. That is where the large cost and energy savings come from.
why_wrong: Safe Testing is about trying risky updates or new software in a VM without touching the real system; nothing here is being tested.
Fast Disaster Recovery is about restoring a crashed VM from a snapshot in minutes; no server has crashed in this scenario, the problem is idle hardware.
Safe Isolation is a benefit that will come along with the move, but the reason for doing it is to replace 10 idle servers with 1, which is consolidation.

questions.q: Cloud computing is often compared to using electricity from the grid rather than running your own generator. What does this analogy say about how cloud computing works?
options: You buy your own servers once, and the cloud provider then supplies only the electricity to keep them running.
The provider ships dedicated hardware to your building, which you own and operate yourself.
Instead of buying and maintaining your own servers, you rent computing power, storage and software over the Internet and pay for what you use.
You install and manage the hypervisor yourself, and the provider only hosts the storage for your virtual machines.
questions.explain: Nobody builds a power plant to run a fridge; you plug in and pay for the units you consume. Cloud computing works the same way: the provider owns and runs the servers, storage and software, and you rent them over the Internet and pay for what you actually use. That is what removes the cost and effort of buying and maintaining your own machines.
why_wrong: Buying your own servers is the on-premises 'generator' model the analogy argues against; in the cloud you rent the computing capacity itself, not just the power to run hardware you own.
Dedicated hardware that you own and run in your own building is on-premises computing, the opposite of plugging into a shared utility.
Cloud providers run millions of hypervisor-managed VMs in their own data centres; installing and managing the hypervisor is the provider's job, not yours.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the five NIST characteristics that make a service genuinely 'cloud'?
questions.explain: The five NIST characteristics are On-Demand Self-Service, Broad Network Access, Resource Pooling, Rapid Elasticity and Measured Service. Virtualisation is the technology the cloud is built on, with providers running millions of hypervisor-managed VMs across giant data centres, but it is the foundation underneath the service, not one of the five traits used to judge whether a service is truly cloud.
why_wrong: Resource Pooling is one of the five NIST characteristics.
Measured Service is one of the five NIST characteristics; it is why a shopping site that scales up for a sale pays only for what it actually used.
Broad Network Access is one of the five NIST characteristics.

questions.q: In the 'Pizza as a Service' analogy, which service model corresponds to take-and-bake pizza?
questions.explain: With take-and-bake pizza someone else prepares the base, but you still have to bake it and finish it yourself. That matches IaaS: the provider supplies the servers, storage, networking and virtualisation, and you install the operating system, runtime and applications on top. The more the provider does for you, the further you move along the analogy toward dining at a restaurant.
why_wrong: SaaS is dining at a restaurant: the provider manages everything and you simply use the finished app.
PaaS is pizza delivery: the provider also manages the OS and runtime, and you only add your code.
On-Premises is making pizza at home: you buy the ingredients, own the oven and do everything yourself.

questions.q: Under the IaaS model, which of these layers is managed by the provider rather than by you?
questions.explain: In IaaS the provider takes care of the bottom four layers: virtualisation, servers, storage and networking. Everything above that, meaning the operating system, middleware, runtime, data and applications, is yours to install and maintain. Responsibility shifts further toward the provider only as you move up to PaaS and SaaS.
why_wrong: Runtime is managed by you under IaaS; it becomes the provider's responsibility only from PaaS upward.
Middleware is managed by you under IaaS; the provider takes it over only in PaaS and SaaS.
The operating system is managed by you under IaaS, which is why the take-and-bake analogy says you install the OS and apps yourself.

questions.q: A team migrates from IaaS to PaaS. Which one of these layers stops being their responsibility and becomes the provider's?
questions.explain: Moving from IaaS to PaaS hands three layers to the provider: the operating system, middleware and runtime. Applications and data stay with you in both models, and storage and networking were already the provider's under IaaS. That is why PaaS is 'pizza delivery': the base and the oven are handled, you only add your code.
why_wrong: Applications are managed by you under both IaaS and PaaS; only SaaS hands them to the provider.
Data is managed by you under both IaaS and PaaS; only SaaS hands it to the provider.
Storage and networking were already the provider's responsibility under IaaS, so nothing changes for them in the move.

questions.q: Which statement about the cloud infrastructure market (Q1 2026, Synergy Research) is correct?
options: Azure is the fastest-growing of the Big Three.
Google Cloud launched first and still leads the market.
AWS launched first, in 2006, and still leads the market.
The three largest providers together run less than half of the world's cloud infrastructure.
questions.explain: Amazon Web Services was the first of the big providers to launch, back in 2006, and it still holds the largest share. Just three companies run over 60% of the world's cloud infrastructure. Each of the three has its own profile: AWS leads, Azure's strength is its deep ties to enterprise Microsoft tools, and Google Cloud is the fastest-growing.
why_wrong: Google Cloud, not Azure, is the fastest-growing of the Big Three; Azure's distinguishing strength is its deep ties to enterprise Microsoft tools.
AWS, not Google Cloud, launched first and still leads; Google Cloud is the fastest-growing, not the largest.
Just three companies run over 60% of the world's cloud infrastructure, well over half.

questions.q: A university's exam-results portal gets almost no traffic all year, then millions of hits on results day. Hosted on a cloud provider, it automatically adds servers as the load spikes, drops them again by evening, and the month's bill reflects only the hours those extra servers actually ran. Which two NIST characteristics does this story show?
options: Resource Pooling and Broad Network Access
Rapid Elasticity and Broad Network Access
questions.explain: Adding servers as demand rises and removing them when it falls is Rapid Elasticity: capacity stretches and shrinks with the load. Being billed only for the hours the extra servers actually ran is Measured Service: usage is metered and you pay for what you consume. A shopping site scaling up for a big sale and paying only for what it used is exactly the same pattern.
why_wrong: Resource Pooling is about many customers sharing the provider's physical resources and Broad Network Access is about reaching the service from any device over the network; neither describes scaling with demand or paying per use.

On-Demand Self-Service is about provisioning resources yourself without waiting on the provider, and Resource Pooling is about shared infrastructure; the story is about automatic scaling and a usage-based bill.
Rapid Elasticity is half right, but Broad Network Access does not explain the pay-only-for-what-ran bill; that is Measured Service.

questions.q: At 2 a.m. before a demo, Sana logs into her cloud provider's web console, picks a VM size and clicks Create; the machine is running within a minute. She never raised a ticket, emailed anyone or waited for a person at the provider to approve the request. Which NIST characteristic does this most directly illustrate?
questions.explain: On-Demand Self-Service means a customer can provision computing resources such as a server or storage by themselves, whenever they need them, without any human interaction with the provider. Sana got a running VM in the middle of the night purely through the console, which is exactly that. It is the trait that makes renting computing power feel like flipping a switch rather than placing an order with a supplier and waiting.
why_wrong: Rapid Elasticity is about capacity growing and shrinking with demand; Sana created a single machine for a demo, and nothing in the story scales up or down with load.
Resource Pooling is about the provider serving many customers from shared physical resources; the story is about how Sana obtained the VM, not about whose hardware it shares.
Measured Service is about metering usage and paying for what you consume; no bill or usage measurement appears anywhere in the story.

questions.q: A hospital keeps its patient records on servers inside its own building because of privacy rules, but runs its public website and appointment-booking app on AWS. The two environments are connected so the booking app can check free slots against the internal system. Which deployment model is this?
questions.explain: A hybrid cloud is a connected mix of private and public: the sensitive part (patient records) stays on infrastructure dedicated to the hospital, while the public-facing apps run on a shared public cloud such as AWS. The link between the two is what makes it hybrid rather than two separate setups. This is the standard pattern for keeping sensitive data private while still using the public cloud for everything else.
why_wrong: A private cloud would mean everything, including the website and booking app, runs on infrastructure dedicated to the hospital alone; here the public-facing apps are on AWS.
A public cloud would put the patient records on shared AWS infrastructure too, which is exactly what the hospital is avoiding.
A community cloud is shared by several organisations with common needs, such as government agencies pooling infrastructure; the hospital is not sharing its systems with other organisations.

questions.q: Five state universities in the same region must all follow the same data-protection rules for student records. Instead of each building its own cloud, they set up one shared infrastructure that only these five universities use; no outside company can rent capacity on it. Which deployment model is this?
questions.explain: A community cloud is infrastructure shared by a group of organisations that have common needs; government agencies sharing one platform is the classic example. It sits between private (one organisation only) and public (open to anyone): the member organisations share it, but nobody outside the group can use it. Several universities with identical compliance needs pooling one infrastructure fits this exactly.
why_wrong: A public cloud is shared infrastructure open to anyone, like AWS, Azure or Google Cloud; here only the five universities can use it and outside companies are shut out.
A hybrid cloud is a connected mix of public and private infrastructure; nothing in this setup places any part on a public cloud.
A private cloud is dedicated to a single organisation, such as a bank's internal cloud; here five separate universities share the same infrastructure.

questions.q: Meera works in IT at a bank. Management wants developers to be able to spin up virtual machines on demand, but insists the infrastructure be used by the bank alone and never shared with any other company. Which deployment model should Meera propose?
questions.explain: A private cloud is dedicated to one organisation only; a bank's internal cloud is the classic example. It still delivers cloud-style conveniences such as self-service VMs, but on infrastructure nobody outside the bank uses. When the hard requirement is 'shared with no other company', private is the only model that fits.
why_wrong: A public cloud is shared infrastructure open to anyone, which is exactly what management has ruled out.
A community cloud is shared by several organisations with common needs; the bank does not want to share with anyone.
A hybrid cloud connects a private part to a public part; management wants nothing on shared public infrastructure, so there is no public half to connect.

questions.q: Arjun has finished a web app for a hackathon. He wants to push his code and have it run on the Internet without ever picking an operating system, installing a runtime or configuring a server. Which service model, and which example, fits what he wants?
options: PaaS, for example Google App Engine
IaaS, for example a rented virtual machine on AWS
On-Premises, running the app on his own laptop
questions.explain: Under PaaS the provider manages the runtime, middleware, operating system and everything below; you manage only your application and its data. That is precisely 'push code and the platform just runs it', which is what Google App Engine (or Heroku, or Azure App Service) offers. In pizza terms it is delivery: you add nothing but your code.
why_wrong: On an IaaS virtual machine Arjun would still have to install the operating system and runtime himself, which is exactly what he wants to avoid.
SaaS is a finished application you simply use, like Google Photos; it does not run code that Arjun writes.
Running on his own laptop means he manages all eight layers himself, including the OS and the server, the opposite of what he asked for.

questions.q: Priya's college design club signs up for a web-based video-calling service to hold weekly meetings. Nobody in the club installs software on a server, patches an operating system or manages a runtime; they open the app in a browser and use it. In pizza terms, what has the club chosen?
questions.explain: Dining at a restaurant means the provider does everything and you just enjoy the finished dish. That is SaaS: the provider manages all eight layers, from networking and servers up to the application itself, and the club simply uses the finished app. Zoom handling video calls for millions of simultaneous meetings is exactly this kind of service.
why_wrong: Take-and-bake (IaaS) would leave the club installing the OS and app on rented servers, which nobody in the club is doing.
Pizza delivery (PaaS) still requires you to bring your own code; the club is not writing or deploying any application.
Making pizza at home (On-Premises) means owning and managing every layer yourself, the opposite of using a hosted app in a browser.

questions.q: Rahul's team rents virtual machines from a cloud provider, installs Ubuntu on them and deploys their app. Months later the site is breached through a known operating-system vulnerability that was never patched. Under the model they were using, who was responsible for keeping the OS patched?
options: Rahul's team, because under IaaS the customer manages the operating system
The provider, because under IaaS the provider manages the operating system and everything below it
The provider, because the operating system is part of the virtualisation layer
Rahul's team is responsible only for applications and data; the OS was the provider's job
questions.explain: Renting VMs and installing your own OS is IaaS. In that model the provider's responsibility stops at virtualisation, servers, storage and networking; the operating system, middleware, runtime, data and applications are the customer's. So patching Ubuntu was Rahul's team's job. Had they wanted the provider to own the OS, they would have needed PaaS or SaaS.
why_wrong: Under IaaS the provider's responsibility stops below the OS, at virtualisation, servers, storage and networking; the OS is the customer's.
The operating system is its own layer above virtualisation; the provider manages the hypervisor and the VMs, not the OS installed inside them.
Managing only applications and data is the PaaS split; Rahul's team chose IaaS by installing their own OS, so the OS was theirs.
